newsitem.title: USA: AOL jumps on expectations of pact, refunds.
newsitem.headline: AOL jumps on expectations of pact, refunds.

text.p: America Online Inc. stock jumped Wednesday on expectations of an agreement with 37 state attorneys general, which is expected to include refunds for frustrated customers, traders and analysts said.

Officials with the world's largest online service were not immediately available for comment, but the Illinois attorney general's office was slated to hold a news conference in Chicago at 2:30 p.m. EST.
New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco also planned to hold a news conference at 2:45 p.m. EST at his New York City office, his office said.
America Online stock rose $2 to $37.375 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Last Thursday, state attorneys general or their aides met in Chicago with Dulles, Va.-based America Online to discuss complaints in the past few months by consumers frustrated by repeated busy signals when they attempt to log on to the service.
On Friday, Vacco threatened to sue America Online for allegedly deceptive business practices and false advertising if its negotiations with the online service seeking relief for customers broke down.
"I expect it (the agreement) to cost them something," said Abhishek Gami, an analyst with Nesbitt Burns Securities, adding that the settlement will "eliminate a cloud over the stock."

"I'm looking at the cost of additional refunds, that's got to be a minimal part of this," he said. Gami said he also expects America Online might incur a cost for more customer service representatives, which may be another element of a pact.
One industry source said refunds are expected to be part of the settlement but that it will not be a blanket refund for all 8 millon America Online subscribers.
Last week, America Online Chairman Steve Case said he was not willing to give refunds or free time to frustrated consumers.

America Online was hit by an unexpectedly large upsurge in the number of people trying to log on since Dec. 1, when it switched its subscribers from an hourly pricing plan to a $19.95-a-month flat rate for unlimited access.
In trying to placate angry customers, the company has promised to spend $350 million to upgrade the service.
"We're comfortable with it. We think it's a good deal for consumers," Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan said.

The agreement, which Ryan expected would be formally signed by Thursday, called for America Online's customers to receive graduated refunds of up to $39.90 based on how much time they spent logged on to the service over the past two months.
Any customer can demand a free month's service, no questions asked, Ryan said.

Under the settlement, America Online, which ran into capacity troubles Dec. 1 when it offered customers unlimited access for a flat $19.95 per month fee, also agreed to cease all new advertising for the month of February other than that already contracted. The prosecutors had complained America Online was continuing to advertise and sign up new customers even as it could not deliver the service to existing users.
